Pandemic Related Academic Impact
• As we are all aware, the pandemic greatly disrupted the lives of people
 worldwide over the last 18 months.
• The impact on education was dramatic with millions of students receiving
 education in new ways.
• A concern of many is to what extent the pandemic impacted students:
 Academically, emotionally, physically.
• The Center has been working with a dozen states to investigate the extent to
 which the pandemic has impacted student learning.
• As part of that effort, we’ve produced some resources that states can use to
 help understand academic impact.
 • Early Academic Impact Findings from Spring 2021 Assessments
 • Understanding Pandemic Learning Loss and Learning Recovery

Pandemic Related Academic Impact
• The pandemic and all the ensuing disruptions functions as a kind of
 “academic headwind”, impeding (in general) the academic progress of
 students.
• Headwinds impede progress in two ways:
 • They slow one’s rate of progress
 • The slower rate of progress leads to less distance being travelled.
• In education these two impediments manifest themselves (roughly) with
 assessments as:
 • Decrease in student growth (decrease in learning velocity).
 • Decrease in student attainment (decrease in amount learned).
• In some states, understanding this phenomenon requires special
 consideration of low participation/changing demographics.

Pandemic related academic impact
• Understanding pandemic related impact necessarily requires looking back
 to pre-pandemic results.
• The natural impulse of stakeholders to want to compare 2021 results with
 2019 results is the correct impulse at both the individual, school, district,
 and state level.
• Wanting to look at 2019 to 2021 change is an attempt to investigate impact.
• The challenge is making 2019 to 2021 comparisons apples-to-apples
 comparisons.
• Supporting these comparisons requires:
 • Doing so in a technically rigorous manner.
 • Communicating the results/comparisons clearly so non-technical audiences get
 the main message. This is the hardest part.

Data to assess academic impact
• During the 2020-2021 academic year, student achievement data from
 achievement vendors (primarily Renaissance Star, NWEA MAP, and Curriculum
 Associates iReady) was all that was available to investigate pandemic related
 academic impact.
• States summative assessments (cancelled in 2020) were broadly administered
 nationwide in 2021.
• Participation rates ranged from normal (> 95%) to poor.
• Given their technical quality, alignment with state standards, coverage of the
 state student population, and long-term history, for nearly all states, 2021
 state summative assessment data provides excellent data on which to begin
 investigating academic impact.
• Many states have ELP assessments from 2020 and 2021 with which to
 investigate academic impact on the ELL subgroup.

Analyses for 2020-2021
• With comparable results we can quantify pandemic related
 academic impact:
 • At the state level
 • Demographic subgroups including ethnicity, poverty
 • Academic subgroups (special education, low/high achievers)
 • By region/district/school
 • By mode of education (remote/hybrid/in-person).
 • Attendance
 • English Language Learner impact can be evaluated using WIDA-ACCESS
 results.

Student attainment
• Across the dozen states we’ve examined thus far:
 • Decreases in percent proficient are most often reported (though
 percent proficient can mask changes in the distribution)
 • Decreases in ELA generally in the upper single digits but sometimes in the teens.
 • Decreases in Math generally in the lower teens.
 • In terms of mean scale score decreases, effect sizes are large ranging
 from 0.2 to 0.4.
 • These are large effect sizes, especially when seen at the state level.

Student growth
• States we’ve worked with utilize SGPs to measure growth.
• States created baseline, skip-year growth norms using pre-pandemic student data.
• By grade/content area median SGPs:
 • ELA between low 40s to low 30s.
 • Mathematics between mid 30s to low 20s.
• Academic impact by grade is relatively uniform. This differs from interim assessment
 results which show nominal impact at middle school levels.
• These decreases in student learning (i.e., growth) corroborate losses seen in
 attainment.
• Decreases of this magnitude in student learning are unprecedented and will likely
 require unprecedented support and effort going forward to overcome.
 • Multiple year time frame
 • Substantial support beyond just getting kids back into the classroom.

Missing Data/Changing Demographics
• The issue of lower than usual test participation in states has led to much
 debate on whether state assessment results are of use this year.
• For all state analyses we have conducted we also performed multiple
 imputation analysis on the missing data and examined changes in student
 population beyond missing data (demographic shifts).
• In all instances at the state level and almost all instances at the district and
 school level, imputation suggests results would have been worse had all
 students tested.
• Because the vast majority of academic impact results examined are bad, what
 we are unsure about is just how bad (i.e., bad or really bad?)
• To use an analogy, we know the patient is seriously sick with cancer, we don’t
 know whether it is stage IIIA, IIIB, or IIIC.

Demographic/Academic Subgroup Impact
• By ethnicity, academic impacts are, in general, relatively uniform.
 • Asian students showed slightly larger impacts in mathematics
• ELL status on state summative show fairly uniform academic
 impact.
 • On ELP assessments, larger impact in lower grades than in middle/
 upper school grades.
• Special education/IEP status in some states showed lesser impact
 that their non-special education counterparts
• In middle school mathematics, several states show higher
 achievers demonstrating larger impacts than low achievers.
 NAGB Dissemination and Reporting Meeting

Demographic/Academic Subgroup Impact
• States collecting data of mode of education during the pandemic
 (e.g., in-person, hybrid, remote) show more impact for students
 receiving remote instruction versus in-person instruction.
• Given these findings many states have prioritized efforts to get
 students back to in-person learning as quickly and safely as
 possible.

Schools and Districts
• Obviously, when overall state academic impacts are large, the
 average impact seen by schools and districts is also large.
• However, there is wide variability in the impact on schools and
 districts.
• For many, the impacts were so large we felt it necessary to add
 the category “severe” to characterize the impact seen.
• In a small minority of cases schools showed modest to no impact
 or even some improvement.

Looking forward to 2021-2022
• As we (hopefully) transition from pandemic to recovery, data from
 2021-2022 will provide an excellent basis to understand whether what
 type of recovery systems are demonstrating:
 • V-shaped, U-Shaped, L-Shaped, or no recovery
• States with compromised 2021 assessments (low participation, fall
 testing, no testing) will have tradeoffs to make in terms of using
 2021-2022 data to assess recovery.
• Using data for these purposes is not the typical use of data for
 “accountability” and requires states to promote results in ways not
 related to accountability. This can be a delicate balancing act.
• Overall, I’m optimistic about the use of 2020-2021 data for academic
 impact as well as to inform recovery in 2021-2022.
